Dear Ms. Martin:
This letter is the Attorney General's order on your
petition for disclosure of records under the Oregon Public
Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. The petition, which we
received on December 6, 1988, asks the Attorney General to
direct Oregon State University officials to disclose a letter
from the principal of the Talmadge Middle School of
Monmouth-Independence, purportedly addressed to Dr. Thomas P.
Evans, Chairman of Science and Mathematics at Oregon State
University, indicating the school's wish that you not continue
as a student teacher at the middle school. For the reasons set
forth below, we deny your petition.
In conferring with officials at Oregon State University,
we ascertained that the university provided you with full
access to your entire file. You were also given an opportunity
to arrange to have copies made of it. The file included
Dr. Evans' notes from his telephone conversation with the
middle school principal concerning your performance as a
student teacher, and the principal's classroom observation
notes. We also found that, although perhaps the middle school
principal intended to follow up his telephone conversation with
Dr. Evans with a letter, he never did so. Thus, the record
that you requested does not exist. Therefore, we deny your
petition.
Very truly yours,
JAMES E. MOUNTAIN, JR.

text:
DAVE FROHNMA YER JAMES E. MOUNTAIN, JR.
ATTORNEY GENF.RAL
SrATEOFOREGON
Steven c. Baldwin
Attorney at Law
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
Justice Building
Salem, Oregon 97310
Telephone: (503) 378-4400
December 7, 1989
Harrang, Long, Watkinson, and Arnold
101 E. Broadway
Eugene, OR 97440
Re: Petition for Public Records Disclosure Order;
Oregon Health Sciences University Records
Dear Mr. Baldwin:
DEPUTY ATTORNEY GENERAL
This letter is the Attorney General's order on your
petition for disclosure of records under the Oregon Public
Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition (submitted
on behalf of Richard J. Reedal of Home Parenteral Care, Inc.),
which we received on December 1, 1989, asks the Attorney
General to direct the Oregon Health Sciences University (OHSU)
to disclose the fee schedules and/or price lists provided to
OHSU by VitalCare of Oregon and caremark, Inc. in their
unsuccessful bids on OHSU's Request for Proposal #17 (RFP
#17). For the reasons that follow, we deny your petition.
1. Background
We understand that Mr. Reedal's initial request for
disclosure of records grew out of OHSU's RFP #17, which sought
proposals from qualified and experienced home care providers
for home parenteral care, including supplies, equipment
maintenance and patient follow-up. RFP #17 requested current
prices charged for selected patient care, but specifically
provided that the chosen vendor would not be required to adhere
to the price lists. Eight vendors responded to RFP #17,
including Mr. Reedal's company, Home Parenteral Care, Inc. OHSU
gave all respondents the opportunity to identify proprietary or
trade secret information submitted with a proposal.
Specifically, OSHU's RFP #17 provided in relevant part:
"Proprietary or trade secret information: If any of
the information requested in this section is
considered to be proprietary or a trade secret
belonging to the respondent, that information should
be filed with the proposal form in a separate
envelope, appropriately marked.•
Mr. Steven c. Baldwin
December 7, 1989
Page 2
Five of the eight respondents, including the successful
one, did not identify any of their proposal information as
proprietary or trade secrets. On the other hand, Institutional
Pharmacy Consultants, Caremark, and VitalCare asked that some
or all of the material submitted with their proposals be kept
confidential. When Mr. Reedal asked on or around October 18,
1989, to inspect the proposals, OHSU made all of the proposals
available to him except the materials that the three companies
identified as trade secrets. OHSU conferred with representa­tives
of those companies to ascertain their continued interest
in maintaining confidentiality and their reasons therefor.
After receiving those responses, OHSU made all of the Institu­tional
Pharmacy consultants proposal available to Mr. Reedal,
because that company withdrew its request for confidentiality.
Caremark narrowed its request for confidentiality. Never­theless,
both Caremark and VitalCare continued to request that
their fee schedules and price lists remain confidential. see
letter to Richard Reedal, dated March 13, 1989, from Anya
Averill, Contracts Manager, OHSU.
2. The Materials at Issue
caremark submitted with its proposal four examples of
services to be provided, taken from the RFP. Each example
described the condition and care of a patient, and set forth
the cost of therapy per day. Only the cost information has
been deleted from the materials supplied to your client.
Vitalcare submitted its proposal in a different format.
Its prices were broken down into major components (~,
medication, nursing care, supplies), and formulated to state
the total cost of care over a specified period (~, 14 days)
rather than the charge per day. In two instances, Vitalcare
also submitted alternative treatment plans and costs. When it
did so, the proposal included a statement of the relative
advantages and disadvantages of the described alternatives.
None of this material has been released to Mr. Reedal.
3. Exemption for Trade Secrets
ORS 192.501(2) exempts •trade secrets• from disclosure •unless
the public interest requires disclosure in the particular
instance.• The statute defines •trade secrets• as follows:
"'Trade secrets,' as used in this section, may
include, but are not limited to, any formula, plan,
pattern, process, tool, mechanism, compound,
Mr. Steven c. Baldwin
December 7, 1989
Page 3
procedure, production data, or compilation of
information which is not patented, which is known
only to certain individuals within an organization
and which is used in a business it conducts, having
actual or potential commercial value, and which gives
its user an opportunity to obtain a business
advantage over competitors who do not know or use it.•
Oregon's version of the Uniform Trade secrets Act,
ORS 646.461(4), also is relevant to our analysis; if information
falls within that statute, it is prohibited from disclosure,
and that prohibition is incorporated into the Public Records
Law by ORS 192.502(8). ORS 646.461(4) defines •trade secret•
as follows:
••Trade Secret' means information, including a
drawing, cost data, customer list, formula, pattern,
r compilation, program, devise, method, technique or
process that:
•(a) Derives independent economic value, actual
or potential, from not being generally known to the
public or to other persons who can obtain economic
value from its disclosure or use; and
"(b) Is the subject of efforts that are
reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its
secrecy.• (Emphasis added.)
The Oregon law specifically includes •cost data• as a trade
secret, while the uniform act does not. See Unif. Trade Secrets
Act § 1(4), 14 ULA 542 (1980). Thus, the-oFegon legislature
has stated that a price list can be a trade secret if the other
statutory requirements are satisfied.
The first type of information in question here is the
pricing data submitted by Vitalcare and caremark. we previously
have concluded that price lists may qualify as exempt trade
secret information. See Public Records Order, December 30,
1987, O'Neill. In thar-order, we concluded that the pricing
data contained in a contract between OHSU and Blue Cross/Blue
Shield of Oregon (BCBSO) constituted trade secret information
exempt from disclosure. We reasoned that public disclosure of
that information could undermine both OHSU's and BCBSO's
competitive positions. Id. at 3-4. we also found that in
recognition of the sensit1vity of the pricing information, both
OHSU and BCBSO took steps to maintain the confidentiality of
Mr. Steven c. Baldwin
December 7, 1989
Page 4
the information. Finally, we determined that disclosure of the
trade secret information would disserve the public interest in
(1) promoting programs, such as the preferred provider
arrangement at issue there, designed to reduce health care
insurance costs, (2) promoting a program that encourages persons
to use OHSU's medical facilities, and (3) providing valuable
clinical training to OHSU medical students. The harm to these
programs from disclosure outweighed any public interest to be
served by disclosure. Accordingly, we denied the petition to
compel disclosure.
The reasoning in our prior order applies with equal force
here. First, the pricing information has commercial value
derived from not being generally known to persons who could
obtain economic value from its disclosure. Knowledge of this
information would allow a competitor to undercut caremark's or
Vitalcare's rates, thus giving the competitor an advantage in
the marketplace. Cf. Gulf & western Industries, Inc. v. u.s.,
615 F2d 527 (DC Cir 1979) (pricing information exempt under
federal Freedom of Information Act as trade secret; court notes
that disclosure would allow competitors to estimate and undercut
contractor's future bids, thus undermining its competitive
position). Moreover, both companies have informed us that they
provide the pricing information only to certain persons within
those organizations on a need-to-know basis. ORS 192.501(2).
Thus, this information is protected by •efforts that are
reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy.•
ORS 646.461(4)(b). We conclude, therefore, that the pricing
information constitutes trade secrets under both the Public
Records Law and ORS 646.461(4).
we also conclude that VitalCare•s alternative treatment
plans, and its statements of the relative advantages and
disadvantages of the described alternatives, are trade secrets.
As VitalCare's general manager explained to OHSU's contracts
manager, that discussion reveals VitalCare's clinical and
operational policies and procedures. Disclosure of that
information to VitalCare's competitors could place Vitalcare at
a competitive disadvantage in the future. Thus, that
information has commercial value. Again, we understand that
Vitalcare discloses this information to its personnel only on a
need-to-know basis. This information, therefore, constitutes
trade secrets.
Nor does the public interest require disclosure in the
particular instance. You have not provided any specific
arguments on this point. Consequently, we focus on the general
Mr. Steven c. Baldwin
December 7, 1989
Page 5
public interest in disclosure of public records to allow members
of the public to monitor the government's conduct of the
public's business: here, OHSU's decision-making process on an
RFP. Disclosure here would not significantly serve that public
interest. First, under RFP #17, no points were awarded for the
price list, and OHSU specifically informed respondents ·that the
successful vendor would not be required to adhere to the price
lists. Thus, access to the price lists would not aid the public
in monitoring OHSU's adherence to its RFP process. Second,
disclosure of VitalCare's alternative treatment proposals, which
were not even directly responsive to the RFP, could not aid the
public in reviewing OHSU's administration of its RFP process.
In addition, disclosure would harm the public's interest
in OHSU's ability to attract bidders to provide services such as
the home parenteral care involved here. If OHSU were unable to
guarantee the confidentiality of trade secret information such
as the price lists here, its ability to attract bids likely
would be substantially curtailed, and the public's costs for
providing the care increased. In our view, this detriment to
the public interest outweighs any benefit that would result
from disclosure.
4. Conclusion
For these reasons, we respectfully deny your petition.
Sincerely,
VL~
PAMELA L. ABERNETHY
Special counsel to the
Attorney General

This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition for disclosure of records
under the Oregon Public Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505.11 Your petition, which
we received on October 19, 1994, asks the Attorney General to direct the Department of
Justice, Charitable Activities Section, to make available the identity of a complainant who
filed a complaint related to Eitel Belau, including an unredacted letter of August 3, 1994,
which purportedly discloses the identity of the complainant.11 For the reasons that follow,
we respectfully deny your petition.
The Public Records Law confers a right to inspect any public records of a public
body in Oregon, subject to certain exemptions and limitations. ~ ORS 192.420. If a
public record contains exempt and nonexempt material, the public body must separate the
materials and make the nonexempt material available for examination if it is "reasonably
possible" to do so while preserving the confidentiality of the exempt material. Turner v.
Reed, 22 Or App 177, 186 n 8, 538 P2d 373 (1975).
11 Your petition was filed on behalf of your client, Lily Ulitech, President, Eitel Belau
Corporation, who made the original public records request.
21 This agency has previously provided your client with a redacted copy of the August 3
letter.
Michael C. Zusman
October 26, 1994
Page 2
1. Confidential Submission Exemption
ORS 192.502(3) exempts information submitted in confidence from the disclosure
requirements of the Public Records Law. This provision exempts from disclosure:
"Information submitted to a public body in confidence and not
otherwise required by law to be submitted, where such information should
reasonably be considered confidential, the public body has obliged itself in
good faith not to disclose the information and when the public interest would
suffer by the disclosure[.]"
The agency must be able to present evidence that there was a condition or
understanding at the time the information was provided that the information would be held in
confidence. Sadler v. Oregon State Bar, 275 Or 279, 550 P2d 1218 (1976). This exemption
clearly does not apply if the public agency requests that information be submitted in
confidence to avoid embarrassment to itself.
2. Discussion
A review of the Charitable Activity Section's Eitel Belau investigative file shows that
the complainant initially approached the agency with a written request for confidentiality.
This request for confidentiality was repeated in at least one subsequent letter providing
additional information to the agency's investigator. The agency investigator, Kirk Harvey,
wrote at least one memo to the file reciting the complainant's expectation of confidentiality.
Mr. Harvey's closing letter of August 3, 1994, confirmed, • ... we will make every attempt
to keep your identity confidential. • Mr. Harvey advises that this written statement confirms
his oral understanding with the complainant and that he had regularly communicated this
understanding to the complainant beginning from the inception of his contact with the
complainant.
In this instance, we conclude that the complainant submitted information, based on an
understanding of confidentiality. The agency's representative obligated the agency in good
faith not to disclose the complainant's identity. The information was submitted voluntarily,
and the complainant was under no legal obligation to come forward.
We also conclude that disclosure would cause harm to the public interest. The
purpose of this exemption is to encourage citizens to provide relevant information voluntarily
to governmental agencies with some reasonable assurance that the information will be kept
confidential. It is reasonable to conclude that this purpose would be defeated and this •
complainant and others would be deterred from coming forward if this pledge of
Michael C. Zusman
October 26, 1994
Page 3
confidentiality was breached. We believe that this public policy is not overcome by mere
speculation that identification of the complainant might help identify the author of an
anonymous, but allegedly, defamatory letter circulated after the agency's investigation was
completed.
Because we find that the record you seek is exempt from disclosure under
ORS 192.502(3), we deny your petition.

Re: Petition for Public Records Order - Oregon State Penitentiary Records
Dear Mr. Haliburton:
This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition for disclosure of records
under the Oregon Public Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition, which we
received on May 10, 1996, asks the Attorney General to direct the Oregon State Penitentiary
(OSP) to make available to you for inspection or produce copies of the following records:
1. Offenders Psychological Report;
2. PSI Report.
For the reasons that follow, we respectfully deny your petition.
The Public Records Law confers a right to access any public record of a public body
in Oregon, subject to certain exemptions and limitations. See ORS 192.420. The law
requires generally that the custodian of public records furnish proper and reasonable
opportunities for inspection and/or copying of the record in the office of the custodian.
ORS 192.430. Any person denied the right to inspect or to receive a copy of any public
record of a state agency may petition the Attorney General to review the public record to
determine if it may be withheld from public inspection. ORS 192.450(1).
ORS 192.430 authorizes state agencies to adopt reasonable rules and regulations
necessary for protecting the records and preventing interference with the regular discharge of
duties of the custodian. ORS 192.430. Moreover, the Public Records Law permits public
bodies to establish and recover fees reasonably calculated to reimburse them for their actual
Michael Haliburton, SID# 11534652
Page 2
May 15, 1996
cost in making public records available, including the time spent by agency staff in locating
and reviewing the requested records in order to delete exempt material. See ORS
192.440(3). See also, Public Records Order, April 7, 1989 (Martin).
Your petition states that you asked to inspect and/ or copy the public records listed in
your petition above on April 21, 1996, but that your request was denied by the OSP Records
Department.
In reviewing your petition with Tamara Blair, Support Services Manager at OSP,
Ms. Blair advises that neither OSP, nor the Oregon Department of Corrections (ODOC),
maintains or possesses a presentence investigation report (PSI) among their records pertaining
to you. Ms. Blair advises further that she has caused a memorandum to be sent to you in
response to your petition reflecting this fact. We understand from Ms. Blair that her
memorandum also advises that OSP will make available to you, upon prepayment of its costs
in accordance with ODOC's fee schedule,11 a copy of the only document in its possession
that appears to fall within the scope of your request and petition -- a three page document
entitled "Offender Profile Report."
Because ODOC does not maintain or possess a PSI report pertaining to you, ODOC
cannot make that report available, and the Attorney General has no authority to order its
disclosure. See ORS 192.450(1). Because ODOC is willing to furnish you with a copy of
its Offender Profile Report concerning you, we deny your petition as moot with respect to
this document.
Sincerely,
ELIZABETH S. HARCHENKO
Special Counsel to the Attorney General

This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition
for disclosure of records under the Oregon Public Records Law,
ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition, which we received on
October 28, 1992, 11 asks the Attorney General to direct the
Children's services Division (CSD) to make available "any and all
information and/or documentation resulting from and pertaining to
the investigation of me performed by CSD." For the reasons that
follow, we respectfully deny your petition, in part because it is
moot and in part because the records are exempt from disclosure.
Background
On or about August 13, 1992, CSD received a child abuse
report, which initiated CSD's investigation of the Hosanna House.
Because Hosanna House is a certified foster home, the
investigation was conducted by a team of CSD staff from both the
child protective services unit and the foster home certification
unit. The joint investigation resulted in documents that contain
a combination of child abuse investigation materials and
materials related to the licensure of the foster home. The
information you seek is contained in those documents.
11 We appreciate your extending the time within which the law
would have otherwise obligated us to respond.
Patrick Talarizadeh
Page 2
November 12, 1992
The Public Records Law confers a right to inspect any public
records of a public body in Oregon, subject to certain exemptions
and limitations. See ORS 192.420. If a public record contains
exempt and nonexempt material, the public body must separate the
materials and make the nonexempt materials available for
examination if it is "reasonably possible" to do so while
preserving the confidentiality of the exempt material. Turner v.
Reed, 22 or App 177, 186 n 8, 538 P2d (1975).
Exemption for Records Made Confidential Under Oregon Law
ORS 192.502(8) exempts:
Public records or information the disclosure of
which is prohibited or restricted or otherwise made
confidential or privileged under Oregon law[.]
The confidentiality protection of any record covered by a statute
outside the Public Records Law is incorporated into the Public
Records Law by ORS 192.502(8).
A. Child Abuse Investigation Reports
Child abuse reports and investigation records compiled under
the Child Abuse Reporting Law, ORS 418.750 et seq, are
confidential. ORS 418.770(1). They may be disclosed only as
authorized by subsection (1), which mandates disclosure to
specified persons, and subsection (2), which permits disclosure
under certain circumstances.
ORS 418.770(1) requires CSD to disclose child abuse reports
and investigation records to law enforcement agencies, the
child's physician, attorneys of record for the child or the
child's parents in juvenile court proceedings, citizen review
boards and a court appointed special advocate in a juvenile court
proceeding. You are not within any of these categories of
persons to whom CSD is required to disclose child abuse reports
or investigation records.
ORS 418.770(2) authorizes CSD to make such reports and
records available to other persons
when the division determines that such disclosure is
necessary to administer its child welfare services and
is in the best interests of the affected child, or that
disclosure is necessary to investigate, prevent or
treat child abuse or neglect, to protect children from
abuse and neglect * * *·
Patrick Talarizadeh
Page 3
November 12, 1992
This subsection permits child abuse reports and records to be
disclosed, for example, to the CSD foster home certification unit
if such disclosure is necessary to administer child welfare
services, ~ foster home supervision and licensing, and the
disclosure is in the best interests of the affected child.
Disclosure is also permitted under this subsection if necessary
to investigate child abuse or to protect children from abuse.
The disclosure of any child abuse reports and records to you is
not authorized by this subsection, since disclosure to you is
neither necessary to the administration of CSD's child welfare
services nor necessary to investigate child abuse or to protect
children from abuse.
Any child abuse reports or records that have been disclosed
to the CSD foster home certification unit pursuant to ORS
418.770(2) remain confidential in the hands of that unit.
ORS 418.770(4). A request for such records or reports from the
foster home certification unit must satisfy the criteria of ORS
418.770(1) or 418.770(2) before the records may be disclosed.
Accordingly, we conclude that CSD is prohibited from
disclosing to you any of the records in CSD's possession
concerning child abuse allegations reported under the child abuse
reporting law. ORS 418.770. Because disclosure is prohibited by
ORS 418.770, these records are exempt from disclosure under the
Public Records Law. ORS 192.502(8).
B. Foster Home Certification Records
Foster home certification records are generally open to the
public. However, documents containing materials that are exempt
from disclosure may be contained within a foster home
certification file, triggering CSD's obligation to separate
exempt from non-exempt materials.
Sorting out the exempt from the non-exempt materials is
complicated in the case of your request because of the joint
investigation by CSD's child protective services unit and its
foster home certification unit. As discussed above, child abuse
reports and investigation records contained within the foster
home certification file may not be disclosed, ORS 418.770(1),
(2), (4), and are exempt from disclosure under the Public Records
Law. ORS 192.502(8). Any information derived from child abuse
reports or records and incorporated into documents in the foster
home certification file would also be exempt from disclosure
consistent with ORS 418.770(1) and (2). ORS 418.770(4),
192.502(9). However, those portions of any of these records or
documents in the foster home certification file that contain only
Patrick Talarizadeh
Page 4
November 12, 1992
your own statements may be disclosed to you, since release of
such information would not undermine the confidentiality policies
underlying ORS 418.770. ~Public Records Order, October 23,
1990, Fleming/Troutwine.
The names of, and identifying information about, children in
CSD's custody who are placed in a foster home are prohibited from
disclosure, except in limited situations not relevant here, ~.
clear and immediate danger to society. ORS 419.567(3), (5); OAR
412-01-165. Because ORS 419.567 prohibits disclosing to you the
names of children in the foster cso custody, those names are
exempt from disclosure under the Public Records Law. ORS
192.502(8).u
In this case, the foster home certification file contains
several documents resulting from and pertaining to CSD's
investigation of you. These documents include child abuse
reports and investigation records, staffing records between the
protective services unit and the foster home certification unit,
certain Hosanna House log entries, notes of meetings with the
certified foster parent and notice that the foster home
certification was suspended.
We conclude that all of these documents with the exception
of the child abuse reports and records may be disclosed to you,
but that the identities of allegedly abused children must be
deleted. ORS 418.770. Specific factual details of alleged abuse
and the identities of allegedly abused children must also be
deleted. ~ The identities of all other foster children must
also be redacted. ORS 419.567.
Peter Asai, Supervisor, Foster Home Certification, Lane cso,
informs us that CSD will provide the non-exempt portions of the
21 The identities of the foster children may also be exempt
from disclosure under the personal privacy exemption in the
Public Records Law. ORS 192.502(2). That exemption requires a
balancing of the privacy interests and the public interests to
determine if an unreasonable invasion of privacy would result
from a disclosure. Under that exemption, your assertion that
confidentiality interests should be minimal in light of your
access to all of Hosanna residents' files while you were employed
there might be relevant. However, we need not reach that issue
because we find that ORS 419.567 prohibits disclosure of the
names of the foster children contained within the CSD foster horne
certification file. ORS 419.567 does not permit any balancing of
the competing interests.
Patrick Talarizadeh
Page 5
November 12, 1992
foster home certification records to you. Accordingly, with
respect to those foster home certification records that CSD has
agreed to provide, we deny your petition as moot. CSD may charge
you a fee to reimburse itself for its actual cost in making such
records available, including its photocopy costs and the time
spent in reviewing the records. See 192.440(3).
With respect to the child abuse reports and investigation
records and those portions of the foster home certification file
containing the identities of the children and specific details of
child abuse, we deny your petition to compel disclosure for the
reasons stated above.

Re: Petition for Public Records Disclosure Order of Oregon Health Sciences

Dear Mr. Reedal:
This letter is the Attorney General's response to your petition for disclosure
of records under the Oregon Public Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your
petition, which we received May 12, 1992, asked the Attorney General to order
the Oregon Health Sciences University (OHSU) to disclose various records relating
to OHSU's awarding of a contract to a competitor of yours (OPTION Care, Inc.)
under a Request For Proposals (RFP) procurement process. That RFP resulted in
OHSU entering into a patient referral contract with OPTION Care to provide home
parenteral care for OHSU hospital patients who desire such services. For the
reasons expressed below, we respectfully deny your request as premature.
Your petition proceeds on the assumption that OHSU's delay in responding
to your request amounted to a constructive denial, thus permitting Attorney
General review under ORS 192.450(1). We do not interpret the facts to be so.
Some of the records from the OPTION Care proposal you previously requested
have been provided to you. Anya Averill of OHSU has asked OPTION Care for
additional information concerning OPTION Care's assertion of trade secret
confidentiality for the remaining exhibits, and has been informed that OPTION
Care wishes to confer with its general counsel for his input and analysis. OHSU
officials have also asked their General Counsel attorney to analyze the issues and
Richard J. Reedal, President
May 19, 1992
Page Two
are awaiting his advice. Thus, OHSU is still actively exploring and has not
denied, your request. ~. Attorney General's Public Records and Meetings
Manual at 9 (1989). (It is reasonable for an agency to consult counsel about
disclosure of documents that appear to be exempt, in whole or in part, from
disclosure.)
Without a denial of your request by OHSU, we have no jurisdiction under
ORS 192.450(1) to entertain your petition. For reasons stated, we deny your
petition as premature.

This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition for disclosure of records
under the Oregon Public Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition, which we
received on December 20, 1993, asks the Attorney General to direct the Oregon State
Lottery to make available copies of records that would identify:
How much total revenue each business in Crook, Deschutes and
Jefferson counties that has video poker has earned from each machine
since installation, and how much each business has earned in commissions
from each machine.
The lottery's refusal to disclose the foregoing information was based on
ORS 192.501(5). That subsection of the Public Records Law exempts from disclosure sales
records and similar business records of private businesses which are required by law to be
submitted to a public body, and which are used by the public body to establish quotas. That
provision states in part:
The following public records are exempt from disclosure under
ORS 192.410 to 192.505 unless the public interest requires disclosure
in the particular instance:
* * * * *
Mr. Jeff Nielson
The Bulletin
Page 2
December 27, 1993
(5) Information consisting of production records, sale or purchase
records or catch records, or similar business records of a private concern or
enterprise, required by law to be submitted to or inspected by a governmental
body to allow it to determine fees or assessments payable or to establish
production quotas * * * to the extent that such information is in a form which
would permit identification of the individual concern or enterprise.
The records you request are business records that are required by law - the
administrative rules of the lottery - to be submitted to the lottery. See OAR 177-100-065(1)
(requiring video lottery retail contractors to submit fmancial and operating records to the
lottery). However, after consulting with officials of the lottery, this office and the lottery
have determined that the sales and commission records that relate to video lottery activity are
not used to establish the production quotas that the lottery has established for certain lottery
retail contractors. See OAR 177-40-040(2) (establishing weekly sales quotas for certain
lottery games).
Therefore, the lottery has agreed to permit the inspection of the records identified in
your request. You may contact Marlene Meissner, Public Affairs Assistant for the Lottery,
at 378-3545, to arrange to inspect or obtain copies of the records. The lottery remains
authorized, by ORS 192.440(3), to charge you a fee to reimburse it for its reasonable
expenses in making those records available.
Because the lottery has agreed to make the records available to you, we respectfully
deny your petition as moot.

This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition for disclosure of
records under the Oregon Public Records Law, ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition,

respectfully deny your petition.
The board has informed us that the meeting notices that you received are the only

PETER D. SHEPHERD
DEPUTY ATIOR..'\J"EY GENER.AL
This letter is the Attorney General's order on your petition for disclosure of records under
the Oregon Public Records law. ORS 192.410 to 192.505. Your petition, which we received on
February 22, 2002, asks the Attorney General to order the Oregon Department of Human
Services to produce copies of:
1. The 1998 report by Richard Varvel on the SOSCF investigation of public
record falsifications at the East Multnomah branch of (then) SOS CF; and
2. Records of the distribution of this report in 1998.
The Public Records Law confers a right to inspect any public records of a public body in
Oregon, subject to certain exemptions and limitations. See ORS 192.420. If a public record
contains exempt and nonexempt material, the public body must separate the materials and make
the nonexempt materials available for examination if it is "reasonably possible" to do so while
preserving the confidentiality of the exempt material. Turner v. Reed, 22 Or App 177, 186 n 8,
538 P2d 373 (1975).
This office has reviewed a copy of the report you requested. For the reasons that follow,
we respectfully deny your petition.
1. The 1998 report.
ORS 192.502(9) exempts from disclosure "records or information the disclosure of which
is prohibited or restricted or otherwise made confidential or privileged under Oregon law_" This
Lynn Davenport
March 1, 2002
Page 2
exemption incorporates into the Public Records Law other state statutes that make records
confidential. Because the report you have requested consists of information about individual
recipients of services, it is confidential under ORS 409.225, which provides:
(1) In the interest of family privacy and for the protection of children,
families and other recipients of services, the Department of Human Services shall
not disclose or use the contents of any child welfare records, files, papers or
communications that contain any information about an individual child, family or
other recipient of services for purposes other than those directly connected with
the administration of child welfare laws or unless required or authorized by ORS
419A.255 or 419B.035. The records, files, papers and communications are
confidential and are not available for public inspection. General information,
policy statements, statistical reports or similar compilations of data are not
confidential unless such information is identified with an individual child, family
or other recipient of services or protected by other provision of law.
(2) Notwithstanding subsection (1) of this section, unless exempt from
disclosure under ORS chapter 192, the department shall disclose child welfare
records:
(a) About a recipient of services, to the recipient if the recipient is 18
years of age or older or is legally emancipated, unless prohibited by court order;
(b) Regarding a specific individual if the individual gives written
authorization to release confidential information;
(c) Concerning a child receiving services on a voluntary basis, to the
child's parent or legal guardian;
(d) To the juvenile court in proceedings regarding the child; and
(e) Concerning a child who is or has been in the custody of the
department to the child's parent or legal guardian except:
(A) When the child objects; or
(B) If disclosure would be contrary to the best interests of any child or
could be harmful to the person caring for the child.
(3) Notwithstanding subsection (1) of this section, unless exempt from
disclosure under ORS chapter 192, department shall disclose child welfare
records, if in the best interests of the child, to:
··~ .
Lynn Davenport
March l, 2002
Page 3
(a) Treatment providers, foster parents, adoptive parents, school officials
or other persons providing services to the child or family to the extent that such
disclosure is necessary to provide services to the child or family; or
(b) A person designated as a member of a sensitive review committee
convened by the Director of Human Services when the purpose of the committee
is to determine whether the department acted appropriately and to make
recommendations to the department regarding policy and practice.
(4) Any record disclosed under subsection (1), (2) or (3) of this section
shall be kept confidential by the person or entity to whom the record is disclosed
and shall be used only for the purpose for which disclosure was made.
(5) Unless exempt from disclosure under ORS chapter 192, when an adult
who is the subject of information made confidential by subsection (1) of this
section publicly reveals or causes to be revealed any significant part of the
confidential matter or information, the protections afforded by subsection (1) of
this section are presumed voluntarily waived and confidential information about
the person making or causing the public disclosure, not already disclosed but
related to the information made public, may be disclosed if disclosure is in the
best interests of the child or necessary to the administration of the child welfare
laws.
( 6) Notwithstanding subsection (1) of this section, unless exempt from
disclosure under ORS chapter 192, the department shall disclose information
related to the department's activities and responsibilities in a case where child
abuse or neglect has resulted in a child fatality or near fatality or where an adult
has been charged with a crime related to child abuse or neglect.
(7) Notwithstanding subsections (2), (3), (5) and (6) of this section, ORS
192.501 (3) shall apply to investigatory information compiled for criminal law
purposes that may be in the possession of the department.
*****
(Emphasis added).
The Court of Appeals has held that "[t]he text of ORS 409.225 plainly and
unambiguously provides that SCF records containing 'information about an individual child,
family, or other recipient of services' are 'confidential and not subject to public inspection."'
Kahn v. Pony Express Courier Corp., 173 Or App 127, 138, 20 P3d 837 (2001). 1 You are not a
1 ORS 192.505 requires a public body to "separate exempt and nonexempt material and make the nonexempt
material available for examination." But the effect of ORS 409.225 is to make the complete record "that contain[s]
information about an individual child, family or other recipient of services" confidential and therefore exempt from
disclosure.
Lynn Davenport
March 1, 2002
Page 4
person to whom DHS must disclose child welfare records under ORS 409A.225(2), (3), and (6).2
Nor have you provided information suggesting or establishing that there has been a waiver of
confidentiality under subsection (5).
ORS 409.225 also permits disclosure to the extent "required or authorized by ORS
419A.255 or 419B.035." For the following reasons we conclude that neither of those statutes
requires disclosure in this instance. ORS 419A.255 makes confidential certain materials
concerning children who are within the jurisdiction of the juvenile court. It permits disclosure of
these materials only to certain specified persons.3 You have not contended that you are a person
2 ORS 409.225(4) limits a recipient's authority to redisclose child welfare records. Subsection (5) prescribes DHS'
authority to disclose child welfare records after a recipient of services has waived his or her confidential interest
within the meaning of the subsection .. Subsection (7) states that notwithstanding subsections (2), (3), (5) and (6),
ORS 192.501 (3) shall apply and DHS shall not disclose investigatory information compiled for criminal law
~urposes that DHS possesses.
ORS 419A.255 provides, in pertinent part:
(1) The clerk of the court shall keep a record of each case, including therein the summons
and other process, the petition and all other papers in the nature of pleadings, motions, orders of
the court and other papers filed with the court, but excluding reports and other material relating to
the child's or youth's history and prognosis, The record of the case shall be withheld from public
inspection but shall be open to inspection by the child or youth, parent, guardian, court appointed
special advocate, surrogate or a person allowed to intervene in a proceeding involving the child or
youth under ORS 109.119 (I), and their attorneys. The attorneys are entitled to copies of the
record of the case.
(2) Reports and other material relating to the child's or youth's history and prognosis are
privileged and, except at the request of the child or youth, shall not be disclosed directly or
indirectly to anyone other than the judge of the juvenile court, those acting under the judge's
direction, service providers in the case and the attorneys of record for the child or youth or the
child's or youth's parent, guardian, court appointed special advocate, surrogate or person allowed
to intervene in a proceeding involving the child or youth under ORS 109.119 (1). Reports and
other material relating to a youth offender's history and prognosis in cases under ORS 419C.005
may be disclosed to the superintendent of the school district in which the youth offender resides.
The service providers in the case, school superintendents and attorneys are entitled to examine and
obtain copies of any reports or other material relating to the child's or youth's history and
prognosis. Any service provider in the case, school superintendent or attorney who examines or
obtains copies of such reports or materials is responsible for preserving their confidentiality A
service provider or school superintendent who obtains copies of such reports or materials shall
return the copies to the court upon the conclusion of the service provider's superintendent's
involvement in the case.
(3) Except as otherwise provided in subsection (7) of this section, no information
appearing in the record of the case or in reports or other material relating to the child's or youth's
history or prognosis may be disclosed to any person not described in subsection (2) of this section
without the consent of the court, except for purposes of evaluating the child's or youth's eligibility
for special education as provided in ORS chapter 343, and no such information may be used in
evidence in any proceeding to establish criminal or civil liability against the child or youth, * * *
(6) * * *
(c) Nothing in this subsection affects the provisions of ORS** *

within one of the listed categories, and so you are not entitled to disclosure under
ORS 419A.255.
ORS 419B.035(1) provides that "reports and records compiled under the provisions of
- ORS 419B.010 to 419B.0504 are confidential and are not accessible for public inspection." It
requires disclosure to certain entities and persons, but, again, you are not among the persons or
entities listed.5 Thus, any disclosure of such records to you could be only as permitted by ORS
419B.035(2), which provides:
(2) The State Office for Services to Children and Families may make
reports and records available to any person, administrative hearings officer, court,
agency, organization or other entity when the office determines that such
disclosure is necessary to administer its child welfare services and is in the best
interests of the affected child, or that such disclosure is necessary to investigate,
prevent or treat child abuse and neglect, to protect children from abuse and
neglect or for research when the assistant director gives prior written approval.
The office shall adopt rules setting forth the procedures by which it will make the
disclosures authorized under this subsection and subsection (1) of this section.
The names, addresses or other identifying information about the person who made
the report shall not be disclosed pursuant to this subsection and subsection (1) of
this section.
419B.035.
(Emphasis added.)
4 ORS 419B.010 to 419B.050 generally govern reports of allegations of child abuse.
5 ORS 419B.035(1) provides that "the State Office for Services to Children and Families shall make
records available to:"
(a) Any law enforcement agency or a child abuse registry in any other state for the
purpose of subsequent investigation of child abuse;
(b) Any physician, at the request of the physician, regarding any child brought to the
physician or coming before the physician for examination, care or treatment;
(c) Attorneys of record for the child or child's parent or guardian in any juvenile court
proceeding;
(d) Citizen review boards established by the Judicial Department for the purpose of
periodically reviewing the status of children, youths and youth offenders under the jurisdiction of
the juvenile court under ORS 419B.100 and 419C.005. Citizen review boards may make such
records available to participants in case reviews;
(e) A court appointed special advocate in any juvenile court proceeding in which it is
alleged that a child has been subjected to child abuse or neglect; and
(f) The Child Care Division for certifying, registering or otherwise regulating child care facilities.
Lynn Davenport
March 1, 2002
Page 6
ORS 419B.035(2) permits, but does not require, DHS to disclose child abuse reports and
records when DHS determines that disclosure is necessary to its administration of child welfare
services and in the best interests of the child, or when DHS determines that disclosure is
~ necessary to investigate, prevent or treat child abuse and neglect, to protect children from abuse
and neglect or for research. The statute places the decision to disclose the records in the
discretion of DHS and, absent a decision by DHS to disclose the records, their disclosure is
prohibited by ORS 419B.035(1). Nevertheless, because the records are public records, the denial
of a request for those records is subject to this office's review.
When a statute prohibits disclosure of records except in the discretion of a state agency,
this office reviews a decision to deny a request for those records to determine if that decision was
an abuse of discretion. See Public Records Order, March 2, 1993 (McMinimee). To find an
abuse of discretion under ORS 419B.035(2), we would need to find that DHS determined that
disclosure was "necessary" to its administration of child welfare services and in the best interests
of the child, or that disclosure was "necessary" to investigate, prevent or treat child abuse and
neglect, or to protect children from abuse and neglect,6 but that DHS intentionally chose not to
make this necessary disclosure. We have no basis to conclude in this instance that DHS has
abused its discretion in refusing to disclose the records you seek.
2. Records of distribution of the report.
Your second request is for records of the distribution of this report in 1998. Richard
Martinez, Human Resource Generalist at the Department of Human Services, has informed us
that no record matching this description exists.
In sum, the report you request is exempt from disclosure under ORS 192.502(8), the
provision of the Public Records Law that exempts from disclosure "records or information the
disclosure of which is prohibited or restricted or otherwise made confidential or privileged under
Oregon law." The report is "made confidential" by ORS 409.225, and you are not entitled to
disclosure under any of that statutes exceptions or under exceptions to confidentiality contained
in ORS 419B.035 or 419A.255. There is no record "of the distribution of this report in 1998."
For these reasons, we respectfully deny your petition to compel disclosure.
